newsitem.title: UK: Violence hits N.Ireland after Protestant march.
newsitem.headline: Violence hits N.Ireland after Protestant march.

text.p: Police came under gunfire in mounting violence in Northern Ireland Sunday as a leader of the IRA's political wing urged Catholics to "take to the streets" to protest a parade by the Protestant Orange Order.

Hours after the parade was allowed to march down a Catholic area of Portadown over the wishes of local residents, senior Sinn Fein leader Martin McGuinness told a rally in Londonderry that Catholics should "stand up for their rights."

McGuinness, whose party seeks the end of British rule of Northern Ireland, said the people of Londonderry, who are mainly Catholic Irish nationalists, were like "the people of Chile, Nicaragua, El Salvador and South Africa.
"The place to be demanding justice is on the streets confronting your opponents," he said to wild applause.
Earlier a Northern Ireland policewoman received facial injuries when a gunman fired on a police vehicle.
She was part of a patrol sitting in a vehicle in the town of Coalisland north of Portadown when a gunman fired a shotgun.
The policewoman was injured in the face but her wounds were not life-threatening, police said.
Irish Republican Army guerrillas or a splinter faction were under suspicion, security sources said.
It was the second shooting incident following the midday parade, which was held over the objections of Catholic Irish nationalists living along the Garvaghy Road of Portadown.
Earlier a masked gunman in a Catholic area of Belfast fired five shots at a police vehicle without causing injury. He escaped into a side street.
Police said several cars were hijacked and set on fire by youths as part of protests which hit Catholic areas of Belfast and Londonderry.
In Lurgan, near Portadown, armed men hijacked a train and set on fire all six cars before fleeing. Further unrest hit the towns of Newry and Armagh.
The pro-British Orange Order was given massive police and army protection and allowed to march along Portadown's Catholic Garvaghy Road.
Violence hit Portadown when Catholic youths clashed with security forces at the end of the annual Orangemen's march.

Police in riot gear fired plastic bullets when youths threw stones and other missiles at the security forces' armored vehicles as they pulled out after the Orange march passed off to the jeers of the Garvaghy residents.

Orange Order spokesmen expressed relief that the parade was finally held to celebrate their religion and British loyalty after weeks of deadlock but refused to gloat over the fact that their wishes had prevailed.
Before the march, police and British troops had mounted one of the biggest security operations the province has seen in 28 years of sectarian violence.
Security forces clashed with Catholic residents when they seized control of the Garvaghy Road shortly before dawn to stifle opposition to the march.
Twelve police officers were injured in Portadown, none seriously, police said. Around a dozen civilians were also hurt.
The Irish government said it was deeply disappointed by Britain's decision to allow the parade through a Catholic part of Portadown.
The renewed violence at the height of Northern Ireland's annual marching season dealt a severe blow to already badly compromised efforts to bring peace to the province.
Chances of a new cease-fire being declared by the Irish Republican Army, which has been waging guerrilla war since 1969 to end British rule, also appeared to recede.
Britain and Ireland, co-sponsors of peace efforts in the province, will not allow Sinn Fein to take its place at all-party peace talks unless the IRA calls a credible cease-fire.
Orange Order spokesmen expressed relief that the parade was finally held after weeks of deadlock.

Police Chief Ronnie Flanagan and Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, said the last-minute decision to permit the parade was taken to minimize the threat of violence from extremists in the divided majority Protestant and minority Catholic community.

"The choice I was left with was a simple, stark choice in terms of balancing two evils, each evil bound to bring about serious violence," Flanagan told a news conference. "I'm talking about loss of life," he said.

The parade, one of thousands the Order holds every year in a "marching season" that climaxes next Sunday, took about 15 minutes to file past women waving Nazi slogans and crowds who whistled, banged garbage can lids and yelled "No justice, no peace."

It stopped en route at a tiny chruch at Drumcree for a traditional service where the Rev. John Pickering blessed the march but said: "We can't go on in this country as we are. We need a true and lasting peace."

About 1,200 Orange faithful in traditional bowler hats and sashes then filed past Garvaghy Road's embittered residents accompanied by an accordeon band which stayed silent as police directed in a gesture of respect.
A spokesman or Prime Minister Bertie Ahern's new Irish government expressed disappointment at the fact that Irish nationalist objections had been ignored.
The two governments have been locked in a three-year effort to find a negotiated settlement to the Northern Ireland conflict and have differed previously on Protestant parades policy.

"When there is intransigence on both sides, two intransigent groups, neither of which would move, a decision had to be made for them," Mowlam told a Belfast news conference in her first public statement for 24 hours.
Foreign observers expressed disquiet the the security operation which took control of Garvaghy road by dark.
"They just kept on beating people," Robert Cushing, a U.S. congressman from New Hampshire, told Reuters.
"There was no announcement of dispersal. There was no warning. They just descended upon unarmed people sitting on the street."
